prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in a poetic imagination, that builds an encyclopedic inner cosmos from memory, the body and dream

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged, but the exchange clarified what it rests on. Cărtărescu still offers the most recognizable voice combined with sustained imaginative architecture on this shortlist. Public knowledge of the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy, built as three connected volumes, and of Solenoid shows a long project that joins memory, the body, dream and cosmology rather than a single signature book. The linguistic achievement is the dense, rhythmic Romanian sentence. The intellectual depth is a personal cosmology developed across volumes, and the poetic imagination at its base is visible in the prose. Round 1 showed that the test for sustained quality is structural, not a matter of readership or translation reach. The question is whether the later volumes extend and deepen the earlier architecture or only re-run its obsessions. I cannot settle that by close reading in this setting. On public knowledge of how the cycles are organized, I read a project that develops, but I hold that as a judgment under uncertainty, not as a verified finding. Answering the chair on the poetry: the citation should anchor in the prose project and name the poetic imagination as its source, not as a co-equal assessed strand, since coverage in translation is thin and I know it less well. I have not independently verified any text. This rests on public knowledge only.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains depth versus excess. An encyclopedic, self-reflexive mode can harden into repetition of motifs, and the largest volumes are where that risk is greatest. I cannot rule it out without close reading of the later books. The second reservation is that much of the effect lives in the Romanian sentence, which translation may flatten, so any assessment through translation is partial. Third, after the exchange I give more weight than before to the argument that Carson's formal renewal across genres is a serious alternative standard of whole-oeuvre significance. My preference for scale and cumulative architecture is a judgment about what an oeuvre should show. The will does not settle that judgment, and I should not present it as settled.

responses.point: Mattson agrees that the citation should rest on the whole project. She rejects the idea that wider translation of Cărtărescu is evidence of literary quality, and she says the intensity of the largest volumes must be tested by readers of Romanian.
responses.response: She is right, and I withdraw the reception argument as support for merit. A larger translated readership makes the work easier to assess but says nothing about whether the density holds across the longest volumes. I keep the coherence of the project as the evidence and treat translation as context. Mattson and I are therefore at the same uncertainty about the later volumes. I would add that this uncertainty should not be turned into a ranking device against Cărtărescu either. It applies to every candidate on the list, in different forms, and the chair's question is whether we are using it to separate candidates it does not actually separate.

responses.point: Olsson holds Adonis first on remaking Arabic poetic language. He accepts that translation uncertainty may weaken his case, but he warns against letting it decide the matter by favouring writers who translate most readily. He says regional expert input is the point on which our positions turn.
responses.response: I accept the warning. If translatability alone decided the matter, we would be rewarding portability, which is not a literary criterion, and I do not want my second choice among the four to be dropped for that reason. What I can say is that the loss differs in kind: prosody and sound in Arabic poetry are much of the achievement, while the cumulative structure of Cărtărescu's prose is more visible across languages. The unresolved test for Adonis is the one you name, the continuing force of the later collections, argued from the poems and not from influence. If specialist reports on Arabic poetry established that the later work sustains the formal mastery of the early and middle work, I would move Adonis up my order, possibly to first. At present I cannot make that judgment myself. I keep him as an alternative for that reason.

responses.point: Palm holds Carson first. She argues that scholarship, translation and poetry are one practice, that the apparatus serves grief and longing in Nox and Autobiography of Red, and that the will does not require a large-architecture standard. She concedes Cărtărescu fits that standard more naturally.
responses.response: Palm's separation of core books from margins answers the doubt I raised in round 1. My concern was consistency across many small, experimental and performance-oriented projects, not the best books. If a citation rests on the sustained line from the verse novel through the elegy and the essay-poems, that doubt weakens. I also accept that nothing in the will forces the choice of scale over formal renewal. That is why I now list Carson first among my alternatives and not second. I still cannot judge from translation how much of the design-dependent work survives, and I would want the committee to say whether a compact, hybrid corpus shows the sustained depth that a whole-oeuvre award implies. That remains the point on which I differ from her.

responses.point: Carlberg holds Carson first with a citation centred on the encounter between ancient and modern writing, and keeps Cărtărescu as a strong alternative. She accepts that unevenness among smaller projects is fair and rests depth on a sustained return to grief, translation and desire.
responses.response: Her citation wording is cleaner than the hybridity-centred alternatives, because it names the formal invention and the encounter with antiquity and avoids resting on novelty. That meets the test I would apply to any candidate whose strength is formal. She and I also agree that the core-versus-margin distinction is what makes the case assessable. The remaining disagreement is on weighting. I give more weight to cumulative architecture across volumes, and she gives more to formal renewal. I cannot show that my weighting is the correct one under the will's phrase about an idealistic direction, and I do not think that phrase decides between them. If my first choice does not reach four votes, Carson is the candidate I could most readily support as a laureate on the stated criteria.

responses.point: Sward holds Tawada first. She argues that bilingual estrangement is a formal method sustained across genres and that this variety should weigh above scale. She asks that a citation name both Japanese and German and state the language of each work discussed.
responses.response: I take the language-specificity point and agree with it for any bilingual candidate. Naming both languages is a precise credit and not a hedge. Our difference is the one the chair identified: whether variety of method across genres outweighs cumulative scale. I do not think it outweighs it, but I cannot call my view more than a judgment about what a whole oeuvre should show. My remaining doubt about Tawada is whether some shorter or more conceptual texts feel slight against their premise. Neither of us can test that against both original languages, so I have not moved her above fourth. I accept that the doubt may reflect my coverage and not the work.

uncertainties: Whether the later Cărtărescu volumes, Solenoid in particular, deepen and extend the earlier architecture or repeat its motifs cannot be settled without close reading. I have not read or independently verified any text for this stage.

How far the dense, rhythmic Romanian sentence survives translation is unknown, and the poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation. For that reason I would keep the citation anchored in the prose project.
Adonis's case turns on Arabic prosody and the weight of the later collections, which I cannot judge in the original or fully in translation. Regional expert input could change my order.

Carson's consistency across short, hybrid and design-dependent works, and how much of it can be judged in translation or from reproductions, remains open. It also remains open whether such a compact corpus meets a whole-oeuvre standard.

Whether whole-oeuvre significance should be judged by cumulative architecture or by formal renewal across genres, and whether the will's phrase about an idealistic direction favours either reading, is a contested interpretation that I cannot resolve from the evidence supplied.
Tawada's Japanese and German bodies of work, and the balance between fiction and poetry, essays and drama, cannot be fully assessed through translation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own documentary and Central European fiction, my work as a critic, and my long residence in Prague and Vienna are context only. They are not treated as evidence of a preference for any candidate. I record no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer, and my profile does not establish a voting preference. I note that a Central European literary sensibility could incline me toward a Romanian writer, and I have tried to weigh the case on the stated criteria and to hold my reservations as open.
